In the south-west of Western Australia, apparently confined to a small area north and east of Yuna. This species was first noticed in August 1990 because of its rigid habit and unusual tiny leaves. The puzzle created by these characteristics remained unsolved until December 1993 when Elizabeth George and Brian Moyle recognized the flowering plants as being distinctive, thus discovering a new species of Verticordia. A hybrid between V. aereiflora and V. spicata subsp. spicata was also found at the type location.

V. aereiflora is related to V. chrysostachys and V. dichroma but is distinguished from both by its tiny leaves and smaller groups of smaller flowers. On the landscape these shrubs are a distinctly bronze colour, but the individual flowers resemble a miniature form of typical V. chrysostachys. V. chrysostachys has flowers on longer peduncles, in larger spike-like groups. V. dichroma has burgundy-red and golden-yellow flowers on shorter peduncles, but also in much larger spike-like groups.

In the south-west of Western Australia, known only from the type locality south-west of Mt Barker. This species was discovered accidentally while investigating a population of unusual specimens that proved to be V. endlicheriana var. angustifolia. Amongst a few slender plants of V. habrantha were others that appeared to be slightly different. At first it was thought that these plants may have simply lost their petals (as flowers of V. habrantha often do with age). On closer inspection it was found that these particular flowers possessed distinct roughly fringed petals, and therefore represented a completely new species of Verticordia.

This species differs from V. habrantha in having flowers with coarsely lobed and fringed petals. It differs from V. inclusa, which occurs approximately 200km Geraldtom further east, in its spindly habit and 'scruffy' apparently striped pink and white flowers with more sparsely fringed sepals. As mentioned above, this species resembles V. habrantha in its habit, leaves and arrangement of flowers. However, V. habrantha has slightly longer narrower leaves with more pointed tips and flowers with broad entire petals, staminodes that are more finely fringed with shorter hairs and a style without any hairs on its stigma. V. apecta is closely related to V. inclusa, which is a larger bushier shrub with shorter broader leaves and neater white to pink flowers with darker centres. The hypanthium of V. inclusa is larger and more hairy with 5 swellings at the top, petals are larger and less deeply fringed, staminodes are more deeply fringed and the style is unbearded.

In September Wyndham 1988 the simultaneous flower- Broom ing of all three tropical species enabled the collection of flowering specimens for the Verticordia Reference Collection and to be painted. This species is distinguished from V. cunninghamii by its whorled leaves without distinct oil glands, and its slightly larger flowers with spreading petals and a much longer, more robust style. V. verticillata is little known despite having been described as a separate species in 1977, and is still often confused with V. cunninghamii which sometimes has its leaves closely arranged near the ends of branches and branchlets. Although these leaves are opposite, they can appear to be whorled and thus simulate those of V. verticillata. However, unlike the leaves of V. verticillata which remain virtually odourless when crushed, those of V. cunninghamii exude oil with a strong myrtaceous odour similar to melaleuca oil. Its cupped flowers are honey-perfumed, have brown stamens and comparatively longer, thicker, slightly warty staminodes. The mature bark on the trunk of V. cunninghamii has a more papery texture, breaking into strips rather than small chunks. Fresh new growth from the lignotuber is elongated with long internodes, thus distinct from the dense, bushy new growth of V. verticillata.

In the south-west of Western Australia, known only from Eurardy Station, north of Kalbarri National Park. The shrubs were first noticed in November 1991 by Bruce Quicke in a patch of bush that had been cleared in 1985--86 then left to regenerate. On closer inspection they appeared to bear characteristics of both typical V. dichroma and typical V. spicata, two species also occurring naturally in the same area. The new plants seemed to be intermediate between these being relatively uniform with consistent characteristics, some of which were similar to the first species and others to the second. Detailed investigation confirmed that the unusual plants were stable hybrids deserving separate recognition. A pertinent factor is that all other recorded presumed hybrids in Verticordia have been either single plants or hybrid swarms showing great variation from plant to plant.

The magenta to maroon flower colour of this species is distinctive. V. × eurardyensis differs from typical V. dichroma in having more crowded, narrower leaves and smaller flowers on shorter peduncles, with a smaller hypanthium bearing more acute appendages, sepals with narveron rower acute lobes and smaller broader petals. V. dichroma var. dichroma is a larger shrub with larger burgundy-red and golden-yellow flowers. V. spicata subsp. spicata is a bushier shrub with smaller mauve-pink and white flowers.
